task.title: Deploy a webhook relay on Lattice Cloud
task.shortdesc: Set up a Lattice Relay that receives webhooks from a third party, verifies them, and forwards them to your application with retries. You create the project, write one configuration file, set three environment variables, deploy from the command line, and send a test event. Allow twenty minutes. Fictional sample written for this portfolio: Lattice Cloud and Lattice Relay are invented for it.

ul.li: A Lattice Cloud account with the Developer role in the project you deploy to.
The {{cli}} command-line tool, version 2.3 or later. Check with {{cli}} --version.
Node.js 20 or later, for the local test client.
An HTTPS endpoint in your application that accepts POST requests. The guide calls it the target.
The signing secret of the third party that sends the webhooks, if it signs them.

step.cmd: Sign in from the command line.
Create a project in the region nearest to your target. The project name becomes part of the relay's address, so choose a short one.
Make it the default project for the commands that follow.

ol.li:
Check that the relay is healthy.curl -i https://orders-relay.{{region}}.relay.lattice.example/healthz
The response is 200 OK with the body {"status":"ok","version":"1"}.

Send a signed test event with the local test client. It signs the body with the source secret the same way the third party does.npx @lattice/relay-test send --path /hooks/orders --body '{"order":"test-001"}'

Watch the delivery reach your target.{{cli}} deliveries list --last 1
The delivery shows the state delivered, the target's response code, and the time it took.

result.p: Your application received one POST with the body {"order":"test-001"} and two added headers: Relay-Delivery-Id, which is unique per event, and Relay-Signature, which your application can verify with the same secret. In the console, the project's Deliveries page shows the event as Delivered with one attempt.
If the state is retrying or failed, see DG-RELAY-103, Deliveries fail or stay in retrying.

ul.li: Read DG-RELAY-102, the configuration reference, for every key in relay.yaml and the limits of a project.
Add a second target to fan out one event to two applications. Each target retries on its own.

postreq.p: Create a file named relay.yaml in an empty folder. The example forwards every event to one target, retries for an hour, and keeps failed deliveries for a week.
postreq.codeblock: version: 1 name: orders-relay source: path: /hooks/orders # the path the third party posts to verify: hmac-sha256 # how incoming events are checked secret_from: RELAY_SOURCE_SECRET targets: - name: app url_from: RELAY_TARGET_URL timeout_seconds: 10 retry: max_attempts: 8 # about an hour with exponential backoff backoff: exponential dead_letter: keep_days: 7
postreq.p: The file names the environment variables that hold the secret and the target URL, and never the values. The values live in the project's environment, so that the file can be committed.
Set the three variables with placeholders replaced by your own values. The command stores them encrypted in the project and shows them to nobody afterwards, including you.
postreq.codeblock: {{cli}} env set RELAY_TARGET_URL=<https://your-app.example/webhooks/orders> {{cli}} env set RELAY_SOURCE_SECRET=<the third party's signing secret> {{cli}} env set RELAY_API_KEY=<an API key from the console, Developer role>

strow.stentry: The HTTPS address of your target
The secret the third party signs events with
The key the relay uses to report delivery status to the console

postreq.note: Don't put a secret in relay.yaml, in a shell history that is synced, or in a ticket. If a secret leaks, rotate it in the third party's console and run {{cli}} env set again. The relay picks up the new value at the next deployment.

ol.li: From the folder that holds relay.yaml, deploy.{{cli}} deploy
Wait for the command to print the relay's address. It has the shape https://orders-relay.{{region}}.relay.lattice.example/hooks/orders.
Give that address to the third party as the webhook URL.
